headings: Silent is not the same as out of the room
raw_text:
# The Notification You Never Opened Still Took Your Attention

The most distracting part of a phone may be the part you never open.

A 2022 study in PLOS ONE tested 73 university students. They completed a visual pattern task over 960 rounds. In some rounds, a notification sound played. In others, a neutral sound played.

The students did not look at or touch a phone during the task. Yet their responses were slower when the notification sound was played. A brain-wave signal was also stronger in those rounds.

A separate 2023 study in Scientific Reports tested 42 university students. The researchers compared an attention test with a phone on the desk and the same test with the phone in another room.

The phone was powered off, and no notifications arrived in either condition. Even so, both attention performance and processing speed were lower when the phone stayed on the desk.

Together, these studies suggest that visible phone use is not the only way a phone can affect a task. A notification may matter even when no one reaches for the device. And the device itself may matter even when it is off and silent.

### When resisting still takes effort

The thought, “I did not check it, so it did not distract me,” misses a distinction: resisting a cue is not the same as paying no cognitive price. Keeping eyes and hands away is a visible success, but not proof the alert had no cost. Researchers interpreted that pattern as extra control effort needed to keep working, not simply as a deliberate choice to check.

### Silent is not the same as out of the room

Attention averaged 99.71 on the desk and 108.95 in another room. Processing speed averaged 98.48 and 108.57. The phone was off and received no notifications, so silence was not the same as distance. That friction may be understandable: the Pew Research Center found that 72% of U.S. teens reported often or sometimes checking messages or notifications soon after waking, and 56% reported at least one negative feeling when their phone was unavailable.

## In one line…

A notification can cost attention before anyone chooses to look, and a silent phone can still matter when it stays nearby. In these studies, muting a phone and moving it away were not the same thing.
